paragraphs: Here we have two quite distinct moral persons, the government and the Sovereign, and therefore two general wills: one general in relation to all the citizens, the other only for the members of the administration. So although the government may regulate its internal policy as it pleases, it can never speak to the people except in the name of the Sovereign, that is, of the people itself. This must not be forgotten.

The first societies governed themselves aristocratically. The heads of families took counsel together on public affairs. The young bowed without question to the authority of experience. Hence such names as _priests, elders, senate_, and _gerontes_. The savages of North America govern themselves this way even now, and their government is admirable.

But as the artificial inequality produced by institutions came to outweigh natural inequality, riches or power[1] were put before age, and aristocracy became elective. Finally, the father’s power passed to his children along with his goods, which created patrician families and made government hereditary, and there came to be senators of twenty.

There are, then, three kinds of aristocracy: natural, elective and hereditary. The first suits only simple peoples. The third is the worst of all governments. The second is the best, and is aristocracy properly so called.

Besides the advantage of the distinction between the two powers, it has the advantage that its members are chosen. In popular government all the citizens are born magistrates, but here magistracy is confined to a few, who become magistrates only by election.[2] In this way uprightness, understanding, experience and every other ground for pre-eminence and public esteem become further guarantees of wise government.

Moreover, assemblies are more easily held, affairs are better discussed and carried out with more order and diligence, and the credit of the State is better upheld abroad by venerable senators than by a multitude that is unknown or despised.

In a word, it is the best and most natural arrangement for the wisest to govern the many, provided it is certain that they will govern for the many’s benefit and not their own. There is no need to multiply instruments, or to get twenty thousand men to do what a hundred picked men can do even better. But it must not be forgotten that here corporate interest begins to direct the public power less under the regulation of the general will, and that another inevitable tendency takes part of the executive power away from the laws.

If we are to speak of what is desirable in any particular case, the State should not be so small, nor the people so simple and upright, that the execution of the laws follows immediately from the public will, as it does in a good democracy. Nor should the nation be so large that the rulers have to scatter in order to govern it, and so are able to play the Sovereign each in his own department, beginning by making themselves independent and ending by becoming masters.

But if aristocracy does not demand all the virtues needed by popular government, it demands others peculiar to itself, for instance moderation on the part of the rich and contentment on the part of the poor. For it seems that thoroughgoing equality would be out of place, since it was not found even at Sparta.

Furthermore, if this form of government carries a certain inequality of fortune with it, this is justified so that, as a rule, the administration of public affairs may be entrusted to those most able to give it their whole time. It is not justified, as Aristotle maintains, so that the rich may always be put first. On the contrary, it is important that an opposite choice should occasionally teach the people that men’s merits give claims to pre-eminence more important than those of riches.
